questions.q:
```passage
READING PASSAGE 1

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the mid-1700s... [full passage summary for context: steam engines by Newcomen and Watt, textile innovations, iron smelting with coke, Luddites, etc.]
```
In Watt and Boulton's steam engine, the movement of the __________ was linked to a gear system.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'Watt later worked with... to invent a new steam engine driven by both the forward and backward strokes of the piston, while the gear mechanism it was connected to produced rotary motion.'

questions.q: A greater supply of __________ was required to power steam engines.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'The demand for coal, which was a relatively cheap energy source, grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution...'

questions.q: Before the Industrial Revolution, spinners and weavers worked at home and in __________.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'the British textile business was a true "cottage industry", with the work performed in small workshops or even homes...'

questions.q: Not as much __________ was needed to produce cloth once the spinning jenny and power loom were invented.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'With these machines, relatively little labour was required to produce cloth...'

questions.q: Smelting of iron ore with coke resulted in material that was better __________.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'This method was cheaper and produced metals that were of a higher quality...'

questions.q: Demand for iron increased with the growth of the __________.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'enabling Britain's iron and steel production to expand in response to demand created by the Napoleonic Wars (1803–15) and the expansion of the railways from the 1830s.'

questions.q: The new cities were dirty, crowded and lacked sufficient __________.
questions.explanation: From the passage: 'This rapid urbanisation brought significant challenges, as overcrowded cities suffered from pollution and inadequate sanitation.'

questions.q:
```passage
READING PASSAGE 1 (continued)
```
Britain's canal network grew rapidly so that more goods could be transported around the country. Does this statement agree with the information in the passage?
questions.explanation: NOT GIVEN. The passage mentions steam-powered boats and ships on canals but does not state that the canal network itself grew rapidly.

questions.q: Costs in the iron industry rose when the technique of smelting iron ore with coke was introduced.
questions.explanation: FALSE. The passage states: 'This method was cheaper...'

questions.q: The economic benefits of industrialisation were limited to certain sectors of society.
questions.explanation: TRUE. 'Although industrialisation increased the country's economic output overall and improved the standard of living for the middle and upper classes, many poor people continued to struggle.'

questions.q: Some skilled weavers believed that the introduction of the new textile machines would lead to job losses.
questions.explanation: TRUE. 'A group of British workers who became known as "Luddites"... feared that unskilled machine operators were robbing them of their livelihood.'

questions.q:
```passage
READING PASSAGE 2

Athletes and stress... [Paragraphs A-F on performance stress, challenge vs threat states, adrenaline, cortisol, anxiety, strategies]
```
Which paragraph contains reference to two chemical compounds which impact on performance?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D discusses adrenaline and cortisol (stress hormones).

questions.q: Which paragraph contains examples of strategies for minimising the effects of stress?
questions.explanation: Paragraph F: 'Positive stress responses can be promoted through the language... visualisation... Recreating competitive pressure during training...'

questions.q: How a sportsperson accounted for their own experience of stress.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A mentions Emma Raducanu's social media post about breathing and heart rate due to 'the accumulation of the excitement and the buzz'.

questions.q: Performance stress involves many demands on the athlete, for example, coping with the possible risk of __________.
questions.explanation: From Paragraph B: 'any potential dangers such as injury.'

questions.q: Cortisol can cause tennis players to produce fewer good __________.
questions.explanation: From Paragraph D: 'In tennis players, cortisol has been associated with more unsuccessful serves...'

questions.q: Psychologists can help athletes to view their physiological responses as the effect of a positive feeling such as __________.
questions.explanation: From Paragraph F: 'helping them see a higher heart rate as excitement, rather than nerves.'

questions.q: __________ is an example of a psychological technique which can reduce an athlete's stress responses.
questions.explanation: From Paragraph F: 'Developing psychological skills, such as visualisation...'

questions.explanation: B (difficulty regulating breathing and heart rate) and D (larger audience, higher expectations, more skilful opponent).

symptoms of her performance stress at the tournament

questions.q:
```passage
READING PASSAGE 3

An inquiry into the existence of the gifted child... [Maryam Mirzakhani, Einstein, high performance learning, Ericsson, Bloom]
```
Maryam Mirzakhani is regarded as __________ in the field of mathematics because she was the only female holder of the Fields Medal.
questions.explanation: Option H from the list. The passage highlights her as the only woman to win it.

questions.q: Maths held little __________ for her as a child.
questions.explanation: Option A. 'maths wasn’t her interest – reading was.'

questions.q: Her performance was below average until she was __________ by a difficult puzzle.
questions.explanation: Option C. 'she was hooked' after the puzzle shared by her brother.

questions.q: As a professional mathematician, she proved herself to be __________ when things did not go smoothly.
questions.explanation: Option B. 'resolute in the face of setbacks.'

questions.q: Many people who ended up winning prestigious intellectual prizes only reached an average standard when young.
questions.explanation: YES. 'Most Nobel prize winners were unexceptional in childhood.'

questions.q: It is difficult to reach agreement on whether some children are actually born gifted.
questions.explanation: YES. 'While the jury is out on giftedness being innate...'

questions.q: What does Eyre believe is needed for children to equal 'gifted' standards?
questions.explanation: C. 'they must be taught the right attitudes... develop the attributes of high performers – curiosity...'
options: strict discipline from the teaching staff
assistance from their peers in the classroom
the development of a spirit of inquiry towards their studies
the determination to surpass everyone else's achievements

questions.q: What is the result of Ericsson's research?
questions.explanation: B. 'he doesn’t think unique and innate talents are at the heart of performance. Deliberate practice... is what produces the goods.'
options: Very gifted students do not need to work on improving memory skills.
Being born with a special gift is not the key factor in becoming expert.
Including time for physical exercise is crucial in raising performance.
10,000 hours of relevant and demanding work will create a genius.
